claims.text: Differences in mechanical behavior among the equiatomic FCC alloys arise from variations in local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion rather than constituent count alone.
Local chemical short-range order and associated lattice distortion fields modulate dislocation mobility.
Changes in dislocation mobility influence yield strength.
Changes in dislocation mobility influence strain hardening.
Changes in dislocation mobility influence failure mechanisms.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has more pronounced short-range order than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Enhanced short-range order in the quinary alloy creates a more heterogeneous lattice environment.
The more heterogeneous lattice environment in the quinary alloy impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy higher yield strength.
Impeded dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy greater strain hardening.
Reduced compositional complexity in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces less pronounced short-range order.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have more uniform lattice spacing than the quinary alloy.
The more uniform lattice environment in the lower-component alloys permits easier dislocation glide.
Easier dislocation glide in the lower-component alloys causes an earlier onset of plastic instability.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary alloys will have lower yield strength and reduced strain hardening.
Relative to the quinary baseline, ternary alloys will show an especially large reduction in yield strength and strain hardening.
Lower-component alloys will exhibit less pronounced dislocation pinning by short-range-order clusters than the quinary alloy.
The quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can all be maintained as single-phase FCC materials after identical thermomechanical processing.
The proposed mechanism applies only under comparable single-phase FCC states, processing histories, room-temperature testing, and constant strain rate.
